Efficiency, therefore, cannot be separated from the awareness with which a medium is employed. An individual may be highly effective in achieving a goal while remaining entirely unaware of the value –or the cost– embedded in the means by which that goal is achieved. He may accomplish more. He may accomplish faster. He may even appear extraordinarily efficient. And yet, if the medium through which he acts perpetuates the very conditions we claim to overcome, what exactly has been achieved?

And how could the introduction of a third party possibly be seen as a means to greater agency?

Agency for what?

"Exchange is never just about transferring something in the present; it is also about what kind of relationship we are making more durable with respect to our future."

The medium of exchange: a quiet reminder of how we think and feel... 

Excerpt from Chapter 4:
"In a fiat system –by virtue of its intrinsic characteristics and what it stands for– suspicion can but arise. Thereafter, an ever-continuing sequence of seemingly random events can but serve to condone the philosophical-political principle according to which “the end justifies the means”, rendering the prevailing monetary system utterly consistent. With sound money also, incentives can change, yet the interaction itself remains unaffected, because the medium of exchange has become neutral again. A change from fiat to sound money, then, reflects a dawning sense of value—or one that is already present."
As Bitcoiners, we cannot afford to carry fiat habits into a sound money paradigm, lest we taint even our noblest efforts with compromised means. Treat every transaction as a deliberate choice to uphold neutrality, vigilance, and what is truly at stake.

content:
Mr. Meadow is a Bitcoin artist and filmmaker in India. He prices the work in sats. The site is mrmeadow.org.
He found Bitcoin in 2017 through a friend and bought some, then spent the next years on altcoins because he could not yet tell signal from noise. He designed for a friend's wallet company, spent time at Deloitte, and worked with a Polkadot India team that was training coders in Rust and chasing funding. He kept saying that path did not make sense. By 2020 the swings had made the point. He stopped the altcoin work and put the time into Bitcoin art: take the ideas in this space and make them something a person can see.
In this episode of Share Your Bitcoin Journey, Bitcoin For The Arts founder Dion Wilson talks with him about that choice. In India he watched coins get pushed by people who could issue more of them, and he treats that power to issue as the thing that breaks the money. He says the rules eased around 2020. Buying Bitcoin, he says, is no longer treated as illegal. Selling it, he says, is taxed at 30 percent, so people buy with rupees and then leave the country to spend or sell.
The pictures follow that idea. For Bitcoin Racing in the UK he made the social posts and a playing card for fans. In the Bitcoin Design community he drew a Cashu note he believes Calle has been using, and a small app that grows or wilts a plant as the price moves. His first AI film treats Bitcoin as a meteorite in 2008. A gas moves through the city, some eyes turn red, and those people are infected with sound money. After that, fiat looks like a plastic skin. He was printing 21 copies of a mech suit that arrives in 2008. Another piece turns a payment into a tennis rally, a ball struck across the net about every ten minutes. Modeotec printed one of his images on a circuit board and showed it in El Salvador and in Germany. He made a mempool picture during the Knots and Core argument about data on the chain. The line on it is about not weighing the chain down.
He found Maya Parbhoe through a Bitcoiner Jobs post. She was building a Bitcoin school in Suriname and working toward a presidential run. He designed the banners. She had them printed and hung them on the school. A wire from the United States into India was costing 11 to 12 dollars before the work was even paid. A Lightning payment does not ask which country the file came from. Clients get a page of prices in sats.
Asanoha asked him for work for a gallery in Denver, through Bitcoin Art Magazine. Another piece was headed to an auction on scarce.city. He was looking at a plebs conference in Goa, at El Salvador, and at Lugano. A short Bitcoin film was in progress. He tells people to catch the film screenings that run the day before a conference.
His note to a filmmaker who is stuck: use your voice, learn, be kind, and show proof of work. You do not have to play the politics of the old market. Be good at the work. On a swinging price, he says zoom out, learn it before you buy it, and come in with a conviction. The presses do not stop. There will only be 21 million bitcoin.
